text:
I think the whole debate over whether mechanical keyboards are just nostalgia or an actual improvement is a bit of a false distinction. In reality, they are not better for everyone. They are a solid upgrade if you want to work with something that feels different. It does help people who do a lot of typing, whether they are coding, writing, or gaming. There is a lot to be said for the feedback from the keys. It lets you land on the key more accurately.
You can get switches to replace them, you can change the keycaps, you can reprogram them, so there is a lot of functionality. So, instead of throwing it out and buying a new board, you can make it your own. People will buy a switch and say, "Oh, that is not what I want." And then they will swap it out. Or they will put in a new keycap set. If I were to buy a new laptop, that would mean buying another keyboard. So, it is something you can build and do a lot of customization with.
So, I do think it has its merits. However, it is not for everyone. It is expensive. It is loud. If you are working in an office, it may be a little annoying to your colleagues. So, if you work in an office, I would probably say, "No, I want a membrane keyboard." For people at home, it is a more viable option. And it is a hobby. You can spend a lot of money in a hobby, and I am guilty of that. But it can be very expensive. It does not mean you will type faster. It does not mean you will type more ergonomically, because your posture and technique are more important. If you type with bad posture, no matter how expensive your board is, it will hurt. So, it is an excellent product for the right people, but not a requirement. It is not for everyone. I think it is more of a luxury and a hobby.
